tagline: Forest hairpins and mine tunnels connect the White Mountains with Clifton.
intro: The Coronado Trail carries US 191 through high desert and forest, with shoulderless stretches and hairpin turns along steep mountainsides. The Federal Highway Administration’s archived National Scenic Byway description highlights that change of landscape and lists 123 miles, more than 400 switchbacks and four to five hours of driving. At Morenci, the road passes through a copper mine and three short tunnels.

The scenic road approximates the route Francisco Vázquez de Coronado took between 1540 and 1542. In 1928, Arizona extended State Route 71 north from Clifton toward Springerville. That corridor later became part of US 666, whose number identified it as the sixth branch of Route 66. In 1974, the mine section received a temporary designation in anticipation of a bypass. The biblical association of 666 and repeated thefts of highway signs prompted the state to change the number. Arizona renumbered the highway US 191 in 1992; the route history records that the proposed mine bypass was still unbuilt in 2021.

Travel south from Springerville through Nutrioso to Alpine, where US 180 and US 191 separate. Continue through the Apache-Sitgreaves forest past Hannagan Meadow toward Morenci. After the mine, the road descends through the Chase Creek valley to Clifton on the San Francisco River.

moments.title: Alpine
moments.text: Alpine stands at 8,050 feet near the headwaters of the San Francisco River, surrounded by the Apache-Sitgreaves National Forest. Mormon settlers named their community Alpine for its high elevation. Before them, Anderson Bush built a log house in 1876 and used it as a trading post called Fort Bush. He sold his holdings to William Maxwell and Fred Hamblin in 1879. The community occupies Bush Valley at the eastern end of the White Mountains, six miles from New Mexico. US 191 meets US 180 here, joining the two highways northward through Nutrioso.

moments.title: Hannagan Meadow
moments.text: Two stories explain how Hannagan Meadow received its name. One local legend says miner and cattle rancher Robert Hannagan was chained to a tree until his son paid a $1,200 debt. Another story credits a coin toss between a young Hannagan and rancher Toles Cosper. The road brought a different change: construction of the Coronado Trail made tourism possible, and DeWitt Cosper built a lodge here in 1926. The lodge offered rental cabins and single rooms, along with a general store for travelers. The meadow area includes trailheads and a campground.

moments.title: Morenci Mine
moments.text: Three short tunnels carry the highway through Morenci’s mine, where the road has its own temporary designation. US 191 Temporary covers 14.22 miles through the mine. Mining began underground in 1871 under the Longfellow Mining Company, with mules hauling ore carts in the early operations. Phelps Dodge began converting the workings to an open pit in 1937. The road changed too: a 1972 bypass shifted its course at Morenci. In 1974, the mine section became a temporary route while a further bypass was anticipated. That proposed replacement remained unbuilt in the route history’s 2021 account.
